name: Tulcea
title: Ultrasonic Thickness Gauging Tulcea | Danube Delta Vessels
description: Ship thickness gauging in Tulcea at the head of the Danube Delta: UTM for river-sea ships, bulk cargo vessels, cruise craft and newbuild-yard hulls.
h1: Tulcea Hull Thickness Measurement and Ship Gauging
intro: Tulcea is the gateway to the Danube Delta, the town where the river splits towards the sea. Cargo ships call for bulk and industrial cargoes, passenger vessels run into the delta from its quays, and a shipyard builds specialised vessels on the riverbank. For an owner or superintendent, a team travelling from India can gauge a ship here, alongside or at the yard, and leave with figures ready for a class surveyor.

highlights.h: Head of the delta, mouth of the river
highlights.p: Tulcea sits where the Danube divides into its delta arms, with the Sulina channel the route to the sea. Ships working this stretch spend long periods in sheltered fresh and brackish water, which leaves its own pattern of hull and tank wastage.

highlights.h: A newbuilding yard beside the quays
highlights.p: Vard operates a shipyard at Tulcea that builds sophisticated vessels for export. Hulls and blocks from the yard may need condition measurement at handover, and nearby vessels in repair or conversion can use the same attendance.

Passenger vessels, delta cruise craft, pilot and survey boats and inspection launches use Tulcea as home. Small steel hulls in freshwater service reward regular gauging, especially around the waterline, bilges and tank boundaries.

port.h: Tulcea and the approach through the Danube Delta
p: Tulcea is the largest town in the Danube Delta region and the last substantial port on the river before the delta spreads into its arms. Ships arrive either from upriver, from Galați and Brăila, or from the sea along the Sulina channel, the navigable route that carries almost all commercial traffic through the delta. Navigation is controlled by the river's depth, which changes with the seasons and with the rain and snow upstream, and by the regular dredging that keeps the channel open. The surroundings are a protected natural area, and that shapes what can be built and how.

The cargo handled at Tulcea reflects its industrial base. Bulk and break-bulk cargoes pass over the quays, including raw materials for local industry and products for onward shipment, and river-sea ships and barges carry much of it. Alongside commercial cargo, Tulcea has a large passenger and excursion trade, with ferries and tourist vessels running into the delta, and a steady presence of Romanian authority craft, survey boats and pilots. The shipyard on the riverbank adds a different kind of vessel, built for owners elsewhere in Europe and further afield.

Seasons set the rhythm of the port. Spring brings high water and the start of the tourist season, summer sees the delta fleet at its busiest, and autumn can bring low water that limits loaded draught. In severe winters, ice in the river can interrupt navigation for a time. For gauging, the quiet months are useful because passenger craft and workboats are available for maintenance and ships idled by ice or low water lie alongside with empty tanks. The overall demand is small but regular, and often tied to planned maintenance windows.

facilities.h: Where ships can be gauged at Tulcea
p: The shipyard is the natural centre for structured work. Vard Tulcea is a newbuilding yard, so most of the steel there is new, but its slipways and quays host hull sections, blocks and vessels at different stages, and condition checks at handover or after modification are a common request. If a ship needs a drydock rather than a quay, the superintendent should check with the agent which dock capacity exists on the river and what a docking elsewhere would involve before committing to a plan at Tulcea.

Cargo ships and passenger craft are gauged alongside. At the cargo quays, holds are available once a ship is discharged, and ballast tanks, deck plating and hatch covers can be measured around cargo work. At the passenger quays, vessels between excursion seasons can have hull, tank and deck structure measured at a convenient berth. Anything below the waterline that cannot be reached from inside will normally need a docking, and for river vessels that means one of the yards on the lower Danube or the Black Sea coast.
list: Vard Tulcea shipyard — specialised newbuilding on the riverbank; condition gauging of hulls and vessels at handover or after conversion.
Commercial cargo quays — bulk and break-bulk berths; holds, tank tops and deck gauged between discharge and loading.
Passenger and excursion quays — delta cruise craft and ferries; hull, bilge, tank and deck measurement between seasons.
River lay-by berths — ships idled by ice, low water or a lack of cargo; thorough tank and deck work alongside.
Docking alternatives — Galați, Constanța and Mangalia for ships whose underwater plating needs a drydock rather than a quay.

context.h: Port state control and the Delta's rules
p: Ships calling at Tulcea are subject to port state control by the Romanian Naval Authority under the Paris MoU and the Black Sea MoU, and river-sea vessels are also examined for their suitability on inland waterways. Because the delta is a protected natural area with strong environmental controls, expectations around oil, ballast and waste handling are taken seriously, and a ship with corroded tanks or leaking piping is a greater concern here than on an open coast. Measured thickness records show where a vessel's boundaries stand.

EU rules also apply to ships entering Romanian ports, including the Inventory of Hazardous Materials, emissions trading where a voyage qualifies and FuelEU Maritime. Romania's membership of the Schengen area means technicians travelling from India need Schengen visas. For owners of passenger vessels, the combination of environmental sensitivity and public-safety duties makes regular structural checks especially valuable, and they can be scheduled in the months when the excursion fleet is laid up.

psc: Paris MoU and Black Sea MoU

jobs.p: Work at Tulcea is smaller in volume than at the large sea ports but varied in type. It combines newbuild-yard condition checks, passenger vessel maintenance gauging and the occasional cargo ship in need of a survey record. Each scope below is fitted to the vessel's survey position, the access that the quay or yard allows and the tanks and spaces that are empty on the day, and agreed with the superintendent before the team leaves India.
list: Condition gauging of a vessel at handover from the shipyard, measuring hull plating and tank boundaries as a baseline record.
Winter-season gauging of a passenger or excursion vessel, covering bilge, shell, tank boundaries and deck plating before the next season begins.
Hold and tank-top measurement on a river-sea cargo ship between discharge and loading at a Tulcea quay.
Pre-purchase gauging of a workboat, survey vessel or small coaster, giving a buyer deck, shell and internal structure readings.
Ballast tank and piping measurement on an ageing river-sea ship idled by low water or ice, using the pause for a thorough programme.

logistics: Bucharest Henri Coandă Airport is the main international gateway, followed by a long road journey to Tulcea; Constanța is a shorter transfer for some routings, and a small local airport exists with limited services. The shipyard and the commercial quays are controlled facilities, so the ship's agent arranges gate passes for the technicians and equipment from passport details sent in advance. Romania is a Schengen state, so the team travelling from India needs Schengen visas, planned alongside the vessel's schedule.

faqs.q: Do you gauge newbuilds at the Tulcea shipyard?
faqs.a: We can take thickness readings on completed vessels or hull sections as a baseline record at handover, where the yard or the owner asks for one. Newbuild steel is expected to be at nominal thickness, so the readings serve as documentation rather than wastage measurement. We agree access and scope with the yard through the owner's superintendent first.

faqs.q: Can a passenger vessel be gauged between excursion seasons?
faqs.a: Yes, and that is usually the best time. In the quieter months the vessel lies at a quay with tanks and bilges accessible, nobody is boarding, and crew availability is better. We measure shell, bilge, tank boundaries and deck plating, and record the figures against the class requirements the vessel trades under.

faqs.q: Is there a dry dock at Tulcea for bottom plating?
faqs.a: Dock capacity on the Danube is limited, and the shipyard at Tulcea is set up for building rather than repair. We check availability through the agent for the dates you need. If no dock suits, we gauge what is reachable from inside at Tulcea and plan the underwater shell for a docking at Galați, Constanța or another yard.

faqs.q: Does ice or low water affect scheduling at Tulcea?
faqs.a: It can, mostly through the ship's movements. Ice in a hard winter or low water in late summer may hold a ship at the quay or delay its arrival. Because we mobilise from India only when the date is firm, we ask for early warning of delays and re-plan the visas and travel without waiting for the vessel to sail.

faqs.q: Can one trip cover Tulcea, Galați and Brăila?
faqs.a: Often, yes. The three Danube ports lie along the lower river, and Constanța is the main sea port beyond. For a fleet or a shipyard group with vessels at several of them, one mobilisation from India with a planned route reduces travel and makes better use of each Schengen visa, provided the ships' dates line up.
